[[Edmund Husserl]] (1859–1938) explored meaning from a [[Phenomenology (philosophy)|phenomenological]] perspective, examining the role of meaning contents in subjective experience and how they relate to objects.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Zhang|2025|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=pDCKEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA108 108–109]}} | {{harvnb|Zahavi|2025|loc=§ 2. Ideality and Intentionality in the Logical Investigations}} }}</ref> His student [[Martin Heidegger]] (1889–1976) related meaning to [[Dasein|human existence]] and explored how practical engagement makes the world intelligible.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Wrathall|2025|loc=Lead section, § 2. ''Being and Time''}} | {{harvnb|Egan|2013|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=oHzouyEsY1IC&pg=PA68 66–81]}} }}</ref> Influenced by Heidegger, [[Hans-Georg Gadamer]] (1900–2002) studied interpretation, presuppositions, and historical tradition as conditions of the human understanding of meaning.<ref>{{harvnb|Sedgwick|2005|pp=78–82}}</ref>

In his early works, [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] (1889–1951) suggested the [[picture theory of meaning]] and argued that meaningful language has limits, leaving silence as the proper response to what cannot be said clearly.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Borg|Fisher|2024|loc=§ Wittgenstein's Picture Theory of Meaning}} | {{harvnb|Logue|2005|p=719}} | {{harvnb|Hudson|1975|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=E4ivCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36 36]}} }}</ref> In his later works, he analyzed meaning in terms of use and [[Language game (philosophy)|language games]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=82–83}} | {{harvnb|Miller|2022|pp=37–39}} }}</ref> [[J. L. Austin]] (1911–1960) and his student [[John Searle]] (1932–2025) developed [[speech act theory]], which examines how utterances perform actions, including those that do not primarily describe the world, such as asking questions, making promises, and issuing commands.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Borg|Fisher|2024|loc=§ Speech Acts}} | {{harvnb|Campbell|1993|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=CTJCiLG9AeoC&pg=PA470 470]}} }}</ref> [[B. F. Skinner]] (1904–1990) proposed a [[Behaviorism|behaviorist]] theory of meaning that focuses on how expressions are caused by stimuli and evoke responses in audiences.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Bagha|2011|p=1415}} | {{harvnb|Lepore|2009|p=1026}} | {{harvnb|Holm|Karlgren|1995|p=23}} | {{harvnb|Lyons|1996|pp=120–125}} }}</ref>

Some [[Logical positivism|logical positivists]], such as [[A. J. Ayer]] (1910–1989) and [[Rudolf Carnap]] (1891–1970), proposed [[verificationism]], analyzing the meaning of a statement in terms of the procedures or experiences that would establish its truth.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Kemp|2018|pp=73–78, 85}} | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=103–105, 110, 113}} }}</ref> [[Willard Van Orman Quine]] (1908–2000) rejected verificationism, proposing instead a form of [[holism]], according to which the meaning and verification of a statement depend on its role within a larger network of beliefs.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=110–112}} | {{harvnb|Nelson|Nelson|2010|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=N-looDKJn1cC&pg=PA10 10–11]}} }}</ref> He also opposed the idea that meanings are distinct objects and words are labels for those objects, a view he termed "the myth of the museum".<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Borg|Fisher|2024|loc=§ Meaning and Animal Languages}} | {{harvnb|Orenstein|2005|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ZEh-AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA878 878]}} }}</ref>

[[Paul Grice]] (1913–1988) developed an intention-based theory that links the meaning of an utterance to the communicative [[intention]] of the speaker.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Barber|2009|pp=84–85}} | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=90–92}} | {{harvnb|Loar|1999|p=547}} }}</ref> Inferentialism, another approach, was advanced by [[Wilfrid Sellars]] (1912–1989) and [[Robert Brandom]] (born 1950), treating the meaning of an expression as the role it plays in [[inference]]s.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=85–87}} | {{harvnb|Speaks|2024|loc=§ 2.2.3 Inferentialist Semantics}} }}</ref> [[Donald Davidson (philosopher)|Donald Davidson]] (1917–2003) proposed a framework for analyzing sentence meaning in terms of [[truth conditions]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Davis|2005|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=LVcTDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA215 215–218]}} | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=114–117, 127}} | {{harvnb|Davies|2006|loc=§ Davidson and Truth-Conditional Semantics}} }}</ref> Another truth-conditional theory was elaborated by [[Saul Kripke]] (1940–2022) and [[David Lewis (philosopher)|David Lewis]] (1941–2001), who analyzed truth conditions in terms of [[possible worlds]].<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Lycan|2019|pp=129–132}} | {{harvnb|Stalnaker|2011|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=fFsb0zfe6PoC&pg=PA100 100–102]}} }}</ref> Influenced by Wittgenstein, Kripke also discussed the [[rule-following paradox]], which challenges the idea that the meaning of an expression is determined by past applications or private mental states rather than community consensus.<ref>{{multiref | {{harvnb|Stern|1995|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=vbhlJUfx9MwC&pg=PA176 176–178]}} | {{harvnb|Miller|2014|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=7GLfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA1 1–15]}} }}</ref> [[Hilary Putnam]] (1926–2016) suggested an [[Semantic externalism|externalist]] approach, holding that the meaning of an expression is determined in part by factors external to the speaker's mind.<ref>{{harvnb|Hickey|2009|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=kxUdCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA37 37–38]}}</ref>
